title: Voting games rigidity, persuasion constants, and limits of strategic stopping rules
summary: This week settled questions across game theory, fair division, and voting. In voting games, swing tables were proved to determine weighted systems uniquely. In Bayesian persuasion, the optimal receiver-utility ratio was fixed at 3/2. In chore division, the worst-case cost of fair allocations was shown to stay strictly below one-half for two people. In strategic games, uniqueness of equilibria failed for publication choice, and static stopping rules failed to remain robust against disguised rewards. Four open implications among discrete fairness criteria were also resolved.

lead.title: A weighted voting game is completely known from its swing table
lead.story:
In a voting committee where members cast weighted votes to pass a bill, standard measures of political power do not inspect the weights directly. Instead, they record swings: how often a member turns a losing coalition into a winning one.

This raises a natural question: could two fundamentally different weighted voting systems look identical to every standard power measure? It was conjectured that this is impossible, and that a weighted voting game is uniquely identified by its swing table among all simple voting games.

The conjecture is now proved. Any weighted voting system is completely determined by how many swings each voter possesses at each coalition size.

The argument links swing counts to classical threshold logic. Summing the swings of all voters reconstructs the total count of winning coalitions of each size. Combining this with individual swing counts recovers the exact number of winning coalitions containing each voter. A classical 1961 theorem on threshold functions then guarantees that these counts pin down the weighted rule uniquely.

fields.name: General Equilibrium & Cooperative Games
fields.context: Swing tables determine weighted voting games. Veto distortion under strict majority reached 5/3.

results.headline: Weighted voting games are uniquely determined by their swing table
results.plain: Knowing how often each voter turns a losing coalition into a winning one uniquely identifies any weighted voting rule.
results.before: Whether swing tables uniquely identify weighted voting games was open.
results.answer: A weighted simple game is uniquely determined by its swing table among all simple games. Unweighted collisions exist on five players.
results.why: Settles the swing-rigidity conjecture on power indices.
results.idea: Swings reconstruct winning coalition counts, reducing the claim to Chow's theorem.

results.headline: Banzhaf veto distortion at strict majority is at least 5/3
results.plain: Power measures can distort weights enough to grant an unintended veto under strict majority.
results.before: Veto distortion at quota 1/2 was known to be at least 6/5.
results.answer: Veto distortion is at least 5/3 for target weights (3/10, 7/10, 0) with weights (1/2, 1/2, 0).
results.why: Improves the lower bound on veto distortion.
results.idea: A three-player target distribution forces equal weights on two players.

fields.name: Mechanism Design & Auctions
fields.context: Persuasion constant was fixed at 3/2. Static thresholds fail for strategic signaling. Sybil-proof procurement avoids monopoly. Concavity fails for forecast pooling without convex exposure.

results.headline: The receiver-utility constant in bit-string persuasion is 3/2
results.plain: A receiver can gain at most 3/2 times their initial utility from sender advice.
results.before: Receiver utility was bounded by 3/2 times prior utility, with lower bound 39/31.
results.answer: The optimal constant is 3/2, approached by slice priors on 2m + 1 states.
results.why: Determines the exact worst-case alignment constant in Bayesian persuasion.
results.idea: Pairwise coordinatewise disjunction schemes match subset counting bounds.

results.headline: Static thresholds cannot achieve 1/2-robustness under strategic reward signaling
results.plain: Fixed thresholds cannot guarantee half of optimal reward when agents disguise prizes strategically.
results.before: Whether static stopping thresholds achieve 1/2-robustness under strategic signaling was open.
results.answer: No static threshold is 1/2-robust. Payoff is at most 721/150 < OPT/2, ratio 450625/930234 ≈ 0.4844.
results.why: Rules out static thresholds for robust prophet inequalities with signaling.
results.idea: A four-player signaling game bounds searcher payoff below OPT/2.

results.headline: Sybil-proof, safe procurement mechanisms exist without winner-take-all equilibria
results.plain: Auctions immune to fake identities can safely share work among multiple providers without losses.
results.before: Known Sybil-proof and safe procurement auctions awarded all work to a single winner.
results.answer: The stake-share mechanism is Sybil-proof, ex-post safe, and admits non-winner-take-all pure equilibria.
results.why: Proves that identity-proof procurement does not force monopoly outcomes.
results.idea: Splitting work and bonuses proportionally to stakes maintains safety and non-monopoly.

results.headline: Quasi-arithmetic pooling score can fail concavity without convex exposure
results.plain: Averaging expert forecasts can fail concavity when scoring rules lack curvature.
results.before: Concavity of quasi-arithmetic pooling was open without convex exposure.
results.answer: Without convex exposure, concavity fails by 23/1024 for the cubic Tsallis rule.
results.why: Shows that convex exposure is necessary for score concavity.
results.idea: A two-expert three-outcome counterexample breaks concavity along weights.

fields.name: Fair Division
fields.context: Four fairness implications were resolved. Two-agent chore EF1 cost is below 1/2. Orientations and connectivity limits were established.

results.headline: MXS does not imply EEF1 for additive goods
results.plain: Fair partition shares do not prevent strong envy after removing one item.
results.before: Whether MXS implies EEF1 was open for additive goods with equal entitlements.
results.answer: MXS does not imply EEF1 for three agents sharing twelve additive goods.
results.why: Settles open problem 1 from arXiv:2502.02815.
results.idea: Identical valuations force an allocation with unavoidable envy.

results.headline: APS fails to imply PROP1, and pairwise MMS fails to imply MMS
results.plain: Pricing or pairwise fair shares can fail standard proportionality or group fairness.
results.before: Whether APS implies PROP1 and pairwise MMS implies MMS were open.
results.answer: Both fail: two agents with three goods refute APS, and three agents refute PMMS.
results.why: Refutes open problems 2 and 4 from arXiv:2502.02815.
results.idea: Budgets exclude top goods, and partition matroids yield balanced pairs missing MMS.

results.headline: MXS implies PROP1 for submodular valuations
results.plain: Fair partition shares guarantee that nobody feels shortchanged by more than one item.
results.before: Whether MXS implies PROP1 was open for submodular valuations with equal entitlements.
results.answer: Every MXS-fair allocation is PROP1-fair for monotone submodular valuations with equal entitlements.
results.why: Resolves open problem 3 from arXiv:2502.02815.
results.idea: Positive marginal items from an EFX certificate contradict submodularity bounds.

results.headline: The cost of EF1 for two agents with chores is strictly below 1/2
results.plain: Fair chore allocation between two people increases overall cost by at most 3 − 2√2 ≈ 0.172.
results.before: The cost of EF1 for chores was claimed to be at least 1 − 1/n.
results.answer: The cost of EF1 lies in [1/6, 3 − 2√2] for two agents, refuting 1 − 1/n.
results.why: Corrects the published general lower bound on the cost of EF1.
results.idea: Reallocating chores by cost ratio adds at most 3 − 2√2 to cost.

results.headline: Envy-free multigraph orientations require subsidies exceeding n − 2
results.plain: Fairly directing shared network links needs larger cash subsidies when multiple links connect nodes.
results.before: Whether subsidies of n − 2 suffice for multigraph orientations was open.
results.answer: Orientations can need subsidies of at least 3/2 for three agents and 13/5 for four.
results.why: Shows multigraphs need strictly larger subsidies than simple graphs.
results.idea: Parallel edges force orientations that retain envy above n − 2.

results.headline: Connected EF1 allocations of chores can fail Pareto optimality
results.plain: Splitting chores along a line fairly up to one task can force wasted effort.
results.before: Whether connected EF1 chore allocations on a path can be Pareto optimal was open.
results.answer: For three agents and five chores, all 12 connected EF1 allocations are Pareto-dominated.
results.why: Resolves the open question in arXiv:2609.32545 negatively.
results.idea: All 12 connected EF1 allocations are dominated by three cost profiles.

results.headline: Weighted PROPX and Pareto optimality conflict near equal shares for chores
results.plain: Fair division of chores according to target shares cannot avoid inefficiency near equal shares.
results.before: PROPX and Pareto optimality for chores were known to conflict at shares (3/10, 7/10).
results.answer: Incompatibility holds at shares (2/5, 3/5), (9/20, 11/20), and (3/7, 4/7) with integer costs.
results.why: Extends the chore incompatibility close to equal shares.
results.idea: All weighted PROPX allocations in these instances are Pareto-dominated.

results.headline: PROPm orientations exist for graphs with out-degree at most two
results.plain: Network resources can be shared fairly when links can be directed with low out-degree.
results.before: Whether PROPm multigraph orientations always exist was open.
results.answer: PROPm orientations exist when the underlying simple graph has an orientation with out-degree at most 2.
results.why: Gives the first degree-based existence condition for PROPm multigraph orientations.
results.idea: EFX splits on parallel edges bound accumulated loss by two cuts.

results.headline: Leximin-optimal EF1 allocations can fail Pareto optimality
results.plain: Picking the fairest allocation among approximately envy-free options can produce an inefficient outcome.
results.before: Whether leximin-optimal EF1 allocations must be Pareto optimal was open.
results.answer: The unique leximin EF1 allocation for four agents and six goods is Pareto-dominated.
results.why: Confirms that leximin optimization within EF1 fails to guarantee efficiency.
results.idea: Swapping two goods Pareto-dominates the unique leximin EF1 split.

fields.name: Equilibria in Games
fields.context: Publication choice equilibrium uniqueness failed for binary and many types.

results.headline: The Publication Choice Problem can have multiple pure-strategy equilibria
results.plain: When researchers choose submission venues strategically, multiple stable outcomes can exist.
results.before: Binary-type problems were claimed to have a unique pure-strategy equilibrium.
results.answer: Binary-type and three-type instances with two venues admit three distinct pure equilibria.
results.why: Disproves Theorem 4.1 and Conjecture 4.2 of arXiv:2511.13678.
results.idea: A degree-9 equilibrium polynomial has three distinct roots via intermediate values.

fields.name: Social Choice Theory
fields.context: Monroe rules satisfy Droop representation. Temporal Droop-FJR separates from BFJR. Apportionment and entropy results were proved.

results.headline: Monroe voting rules satisfy Droop proportional representation axioms
results.plain: Classic committee voting rules guarantee fair representation to cohesive voter groups.
results.before: Monroe was known to satisfy Droop-JR only when committee size divides voter count.
results.answer: Monroe satisfies Droop-JR universally. When k + 1 divides n, Droop Monroe satisfies Droop-PJR+.
results.why: Settles open representation entries in arXiv:2508.00811.
results.idea: Unsatisfied voter groups exceeding Droop quotas allow score-increasing swaps.

results.headline: Droop-FJR does not imply BFJR in temporal voting
results.plain: Fair representation in each round does not guarantee balanced representation over time.
results.before: Whether Droop-FJR implies BFJR in temporal voting was open.
results.answer: Droop-FJR does not imply BFJR in a four-voter six-round instance.
results.why: Answers the question in Appendix A.3 of arXiv:2505.22513 negatively.
results.idea: Electing one candidate each round satisfies Droop-FJR but breaches temporal balance.

results.headline: Geometric Plackett–Luce choice model has linear entropy
results.plain: The randomness of rankings under geometric preferences grows only linearly with candidate count.
results.before: Entropy O(m) was conjectured for all geometric decay parameters in (0, 1).
results.answer: Entropy is at most C(φ)·m with C(φ) = log(1/(1 − φ)) + log(1/φ)·φ/(1 − φ)².
results.why: Proves the average-case sorting conjecture from AAAI 2021.
results.idea: Bounded entropy at each choice step sums linearly by the chain rule.

results.headline: Quota and population monotonicity conflict at a common house size
results.plain: Fair legislative seat allocation cannot simultaneously match population shares and prevent paradoxes.
results.before: Quota and population monotonicity were known incompatible across differing house sizes.
results.answer: Incompatibility holds at a fixed house size of 8 across twelve population profiles.
results.why: Strengthens the four-state apportionment impossibility to a single house size.
results.idea: A pruned search eliminates all 13,824 quota-compliant assignments.

fields.name: Matching & Market Design
fields.context: Hollow-Shell blocking pairs were bounded by ⌊(n−1)²/4⌋. Safe manipulation was demonstrated with three known agents.

results.headline: Hollow-Shell market has at most ⌊(n−1)²/4⌋ blocking pairs
results.plain: Circular marriage markets with conflicting preferences produce at most a quadratic number of unstable pairs.
results.before: The Shield-Core conjecture claimed maximum blocking pairs equal ⌊(n−1)²/4⌋.
results.answer: Every matching in the Hollow-Shell market C_n has at most ⌊(n−1)²/4⌋ blocking pairs.
results.why: Settles the upper half of the Shield-Core conjecture from arXiv:2609.17418.
results.idea: Cutting circular arcs bounds nested blocking pairs by k(n − 1 − k) ≤ ⌊(n−1)²/4⌋.

results.headline: Deferred acceptance is safely manipulable with knowledge of three agents
results.plain: In matching markets, a participant knowing three others' preferences can safely cheat.
results.before: It was conjectured that safe manipulation requires knowing at least five agents.
results.answer: In a 3×3 market, an agent knowing three agents safely manipulates deferred acceptance.
results.why: Disproves the conjecture in arXiv:2502.18805 that safe manipulation requires five agents.
results.idea: An explicit 3×3 profile yields profitable manipulation without risk of worse matches.

fields.name: Elementary Number Theory
fields.context: Weakly consecutive sequences of prime-power length begin or end with 1.

results.headline: Weakly consecutive sequences of prime-power length begin or end with 1
results.plain: Permutations with repeating divisibility patterns must place 1 at an end for prime powers.
results.before: Every weakly consecutive sequence was conjectured to begin or end with 1.
results.answer: The conjecture holds for prime powers: end terms must divide length and be coprime.
results.why: Proves the prime-power case of Conjecture 5.2 in arXiv:2401.09497.
results.idea: Residue counting forces 1 to an end position when length is a prime power.

fields.name: Combinatorial Games
fields.context: Catch-Up draws for N up to 11 and parity results were formalized.

results.headline: Catch-Up draws for N up to 11 and parity theorems are formalized
results.plain: Calculations determining when an alternating-lead number game ends in a tie were checked.
results.before: Catch-Up was computed up to N = 20, observing draws only for even triangular sums.
results.answer: Lean checks that odd sums yield no draws, and verifies draws on {1, …, N} for N = 3, 4, 7, 8, 11.
results.why: Formally checks the computations and parity characterization of Catch-Up.
results.idea: A pruned search proven equivalent to minimax checks outcomes in the kernel.

outlook: Does every simple voting profile admit a matching with at least ⌊(n−1)²/4⌋ blocking pairs in the stable marriage problem?
Can a dynamic threshold stopping policy achieve 1/2-robustness against strategic reward signaling?
Does every weakly consecutive permutation begin or end with 1 for arbitrary sequence lengths?
Does the game Catch-Up on {1, …, N} always end in a draw whenever the triangular number is even?
Is the worst-case cost of EF1 for two agents with chores exactly 1/6?

glossary.meaning: AnyPrice share: the value an agent can secure against every price vector summing to 1, buying any bundle within its entitlement.
BFJR: a temporal representation axiom, stronger than Droop-FJR
Epistemic EF1: for each agent, the items it does not hold can be redistributed among the others so that the agent is EF1 towards all of them.
Envy-free up to one item: any envy disappears once some single item is removed (a good from the envied bundle, or a chore from the envious agent's own).
Envy-free up to any item: envy disappears whichever single item is removed (any good from the envied bundle, or any chore from the envious agent's own).
Extended justified representation: in a group of ℓ·n/k voters who agree on ℓ candidates, some single member approves at least ℓ committee members.
Fully justified representation: a strengthening of EJR to groups that only partly agree, each member approving enough of a common set of candidates.
Justified representation: every group of at least n/k voters approving a common candidate has a member who approves some committee member. Droop versions use n/(k + 1) in place of n/k.
Maximin share: the best value an agent can guarantee by splitting all items into n bundles and receiving the worst one.
Minimum EFX share: the least value an agent receives in any allocation in which it is EFX towards every other agent.
The optimum: the best value achievable, used as the benchmark.
Proportional justified representation: a group of ℓ·n/k voters who agree on ℓ candidates approves, between its members, at least ℓ committee members.
PJR+: like PJR, but triggered by any unelected candidate the whole group approves, which makes it checkable in polynomial time.
Pairwise maximin share: for every two agents, re-splitting their combined items into two bundles could not give either one a better worst bundle.
Proportional up to one item: proportionality holds once a single item is added to the agent's bundle (goods) or removed from it (chores).
Proportional up to the maximin item: an agent's bundle, plus the largest of the least valuable items in the other agents' bundles, reaches its proportional share.
Proportional up to any item: for chores, removing any single chore from an agent's bundle brings its cost down to its proportional share.

zh.title: 投票博弈的刚性、说服常数以及策略性停止规则的局限
zh.summary: 本周解决了博弈论、公平分配和投票领域的多个问题。在投票博弈中，证明了关键投票表能唯一确定加权系统。在贝叶斯说服中，接收者的最优效用比被确定为3/2。在家务分配中，双人公平分配的最坏情况成本被证明严格低于二分之一。在策略博弈中，发表选择问题的均衡唯一性被推翻，静态停止规则在伪装奖励下也无法保持稳健。离散公平性标准之间的四项未决推导关系也得以解决。

lead.title: 加权投票博弈可由其关键投票表完全确定
lead.story:
在通过法案需要成员投出加权选票的投票委员会中，衡量政治权力的标准指标并不直接考察权重。相反，它们记录的是关键投票：成员将败选联盟转变为胜选联盟的频次。

这引出了一个自然的问题：两个本质上不同的加权投票系统，在所有标准权力指标下是否可能完全相同？此前有猜想认为这是不可能的，在所有简单投票博弈中，加权投票博弈可由其关键投票表唯一确定。

该猜想现已获证。任何加权投票系统都完全由每位投票者在各个联盟规模下所拥有的关键投票次数决定。

该证明将关键投票计数与经典阈值逻辑联系起来。将所有投票者的关键投票数相加，可以重构出各个规模下获胜联盟的总数。将其与个人的关键投票数相结合，便能复原包含每位投票者的获胜联盟的精确数量。1961年关于阈值函数的一项经典定理随后保证了这些计数能唯一确定加权规则。

results.headline: 加权投票博弈由其关键投票表唯一确定
results.plain: 获知每位投票者将败选联盟转变为胜选联盟的频次，便能唯一确定任何加权投票规则。

results.headline: 严格多数决下的班扎夫否决权失真至少为5/3
results.plain: 权力指标对权重的失真程度，足以在严格多数决下赋予意料之外的否决权。

results.headline: 比特串说服中的接收者效用常数为3/2
results.plain: 接收者从发送者的建议中最多只能获得其初始效用的3/2倍。

results.headline: 策略性奖励信号传递下静态阈值无法达到1/2稳健性
results.plain: 当参与者策略性地伪装奖励时，固定阈值无法保证获得最优奖励的一半。

results.headline: 存在防女巫攻击、安全且无赢者通吃均衡的采购机制
results.plain: 免受虚假身份影响的拍卖可以安全地在多个供应商之间分担工作且不产生亏损。

results.headline: 缺乏凸风险敞口时拟算术汇聚评分可能不满足凹性
results.plain: 当评分规则缺乏曲率时，对专家预测进行平均可能无法保证凹性。

results.headline: 可加物品下MXS不蕴涵EEF1
results.plain: 公平划分份额无法防止在移除一件物品后仍存在强烈嫉妒。

results.headline: APS不蕴涵PROP1且成对MMS不蕴涵MMS
results.plain: 定价或成对公平份额可能无法满足标准的比例性或群体公平性。

results.headline: 次模估值下MXS蕴涵PROP1
results.plain: 公平划分份额可确保没有任何人觉得自己的亏损超过一件物品。

results.headline: 两人分担家务时EF1的成本严格低于1/2
results.plain: 两人之间的公平家务分配使总成本增加最多3 − 2√2 ≈ 0.172。

results.headline: 多重图的无嫉妒定向所需补贴超过n − 2
results.plain: 当节点间存在多条连接时，公平地为共享网络链路定向需要更多的现金补贴。

results.headline: 连通的家务EF1分配可能不满足帕累托最优
results.plain: 沿一条线至多差一项任务地公平划分家务，可能会导致付出徒劳的努力。

results.headline: 家务分配中加权PROPX与帕累托最优在接近均等份额时发生冲突
results.plain: 按照目标份额公平分配家务在接近均等份额时无法避免效率损失。

results.headline: 出度至多为2的图存在PROPm定向
results.plain: 当链路能够以低出度进行定向时，网络资源可以得到公平共享。

results.headline: 字典序极大极小最优的EF1分配可能不满足帕累托最优
results.plain: 在近似无嫉妒的方案中挑选最公平的分配，可能会产生无效率的结果。

results.headline: 论文发表选择问题可能存在多个纯策略均衡
results.plain: 当研究人员策略性地选择投稿期刊时，可能会存在多个稳定结果。

results.headline: 门罗投票规则满足德鲁普比例代表制公理
results.plain: 经典委员会投票规则保证了有凝聚力的选民群体获得公平代表权。

results.headline: 时序投票中Droop-FJR不蕴涵BFJR
results.plain: 每一轮中的公平代表权并不能保证跨时间的均衡代表权。

results.headline: 几何普拉凯特-卢斯选择模型具有线性熵
results.plain: 在几何偏好下，排名的随机性随候选人数量仅呈线性增长。

results.headline: 配额与人口单调性在同一议席规模下发生冲突
results.plain: 公平的立法席位分配无法在符合人口份额的同时避免悖论。

results.headline: 空壳市场至多有⌊(n−1)²/4⌋个阻塞对
results.plain: 偏好冲突的环形婚姻市场至多产生二次方数量的不稳定配对。

results.headline: 获知3名参与者信息时延迟接受算法可被安全操纵
results.plain: 在匹配市场中，获知其他3人偏好的参与者可以安全地作弊。

results.headline: 素数幂长度的弱连续序列以1开头或结尾
results.plain: 具有重复整除模式的排列在长度为素数幂时必须将1置于端点。

results.headline: N至多为11时的追赶博弈平局及奇偶性定理完成形式化验证
results.plain: 检验了确定交替领先数字博弈何时以平局结束的计算。

outlook: 在稳定婚姻问题中，是否每个简单投票配置文件都存在一个至少具有⌊(n−1)²/4⌋个阻塞对的匹配？
动态阈值停止策略能否在策略性奖励信号传递下达到1/2稳健性？
对于任意序列长度，是否每个弱连续排列都以1开头或结尾？
在{1, …, N}上的追赶博弈中，只要三角形数为偶数，博弈是否总是以平局结束？
两人分担家务时，EF1的最坏情况成本是否恰好为1/6？

glossary.meaning: 任意价格份额：参与者在总和为1的任意价格向量下，购买其应得权益内的任意物品束所能保证获得的价值。
BFJR：一种时序代表制公理，强于Droop-FJR。
认知无嫉妒至多差一件物品：对每位参与者而言，其未持有的物品可以在其他人之间重新分配，使得该参与者对所有人均满足EF1。
无嫉妒至多差一件物品：一旦移除某个单件物品（从被嫉妒者的物品束中移除一件好物品，或从嫉妒者自己的物品束中移除一件家务），任何嫉妒都会消除。
完全合理代表性：扩展合理代表性（EJR）的强化版本，适用于仅部分达成一致的选民群体，要求每位成员都赞同候选人公共集合中的足够多候选人。
